energy.overview: Private advanced-nuclear developers are racing on parallel tracks -- molten-salt (Kairos), sodium-fast (TerraPower), and site-development plays (Elementl, ENTRA1) -- all leaning on the Tennessee Valley Authority as an anchor utility partner, while fusion startups span inertial (Inertia), tokamak (Commonwealth Fusion) and stellarator (Type One) approaches at very different maturity levels. Long-duration storage is more commercially proven, with iron-air (Form Energy) and thermal-battery (Antora, Fourth Power) developers moving from pilots to gigawatt-hour-scale commercial deployments backed by hyperscaler capital.

cooling.overview: The private cooling landscape splits into two-phase/microfluidic direct-to-chip specialists chasing extreme chip densities, tank-based immersion players targeting colocation and edge use cases, and legacy precision-air/enclosure manufacturers now retrofitting liquid capabilities onto decades-old product lines. Two-phase direct-to-chip is the most commercially mature of the venture-backed approaches, with ZutaCore and Accelsius both shipping at scale, while immersion and microfluidic cooling remain earlier-stage bets with smaller deployment bases.

power.overview: Private activity in this layer splits into three distinct bets: software-based demand flexibility that lets data centers dynamically throttle load to ease interconnection queues (Amperon, Emerald AI, Verrus), behind-the-meter generation and alternative storage chemistries that bypass grid constraints entirely (VoltaGrid, EnerVenue), and fabless backside/vertical power delivery silicon aimed at the chip-to-board bottleneck (AmberSemi). The flexibility-software approach is furthest along commercially, the alternative-storage and behind-the-meter generation bets are scaling with large capital raises, and vertical power delivery silicon is only now moving from tape-out to first shipments. That same synchronization problem -- several hyperscalers hitting operational readiness in the same window, overwhelming physics-constrained equipment lead times rather than any single company's capacity -- is exactly what the grid-flexibility software bets (Amperon, Emerald AI, Verrus) are underwriting: if new transformer capacity can't arrive fast enough, squeezing more out of the existing grid becomes the only lever left.

silicon.overview: Around the memory/fab bottleneck, private companies are pursuing three distinct bets: optical/photonic interconnect firms trying to move data between compute and memory faster than copper allows, analog in-memory-compute startups trying to collapse the logic/memory split outright, and a small set of alternative foundries and materials/OSAT suppliers trying to diversify capacity away from the TSMC/Samsung/SK Hynix/Micron core. Most of these remain pre-revenue or early-commercial, while the alternative-foundry and materials players are further along but still years from meaningful share.

compute.overview: The private AI-compute field splits into three distinct bets: dataflow/wafer-scale inference specialists (SambaNova, Tenstorrent) racing to reach massive scale via mega-rounds or acquisition before running out of runway; ex-chipmakers pivoting into GPU-neocloud businesses (Groq, Lambda) rather than competing on silicon alone; and early-stage analog/in-memory architectures (EnCharge AI) still proving out efficiency claims at small volume. Cerebras, formerly the highest-profile name in this group, has since gone public, underscoring how fast the leaders in this space are exiting private markets.

networking.overview: The private networking layer clusters around co-packaged optics chiplet approaches (Ayar Labs, Lightmatter), specialized multi-wavelength laser sources feeding those fabrics (Xscape Photonics), cryogenic digital control chips bridging quantum and classical compute (SEEQC), and AI hardware startups repositioning around inference services (Groq). Juniper Networks is no longer an independent private company, having been fully absorbed into HPE's networking business. Maturity varies widely: CPO chiplets are moving into paid production runs, laser sources remain earlier-stage Series A technology, and quantum control chips are still pre-commercial validation.

serversdc.overview: The private data center landscape splits between capital-hungry hyperscale wholesale developers racing to lock in gigawatt-scale land and power, and already-consolidated PE/sovereign-owned colocation platforms now weighing public listings to access permanent capital. A parallel Nordic/European colocation tier (atNorth) is being absorbed into larger public-private consortia as sovereign AI and data-residency demand grows.

cloud.overview: Private neocloud capacity providers split into vertically-integrated developers that build their own power and data centers (Crusoe, Nscale), pure GPU-rental clouds racing toward public listings (Lambda), and inference-specialized operators pivoting business models entirely (Groq). Maturity varies widely: Nscale and Lambda are IPO-ready with tens of billions in contracted revenue, while smaller entrants like Firmus and Sharon AI are still scaling through vendor-backed financing that Nvidia itself has recently started pulling back.

applications.overview: The frontier-lab tier (OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, Mistral) is now defined by pre-IPO positioning and massive capital raises rather than pure research competition, while enterprise tool makers (Harvey, Glean) are proving out vertical-specific ARR at multi-hundred-million to billion-dollar scale. Consumer app makers (Perplexity, Midjourney) sit furthest from monetization certainty, still balancing rapid usage growth against legal risk and thin differentiation from bundled incumbent assistants.
